lessons.title: The MSME 45-Day Payment Rule and What It Means for Buyers

children.text: Every previous lesson treated supplier payment terms as a commercial negotiation. For one category of supplier in India, it is not. If your supplier is a registered micro or small enterprise, the maximum credit period is set by law, the interest for exceeding it is set by law at a punitive rate, and the tax consequence of still owing the money on 31 March is severe.
This lesson is written for the buyer, because that is where the exposure sits. If you are on the supplier side, the same rules are your strongest collection tool.

protects registered micro and small enterprises. Medium enterprises are outside the payment timeline entirely, which surprises most people. The classification thresholds were revised with effect from 1 April 2025.

markDefs.definition: The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006, which sets the payment timelines and interest consequences for buyers dealing with registered micro and small suppliers.

body.caption: MSME classification from 1 April 2025 (composite criterion, both conditions apply)
headers: Investment in plant, machinery or equipment

body.text: Two practical traps. First, the supplier must actually be registered, so you need its Udyam registration number and category on record, ideally collected at vendor onboarding and refreshed annually, since a supplier can move from micro to small to medium as it grows. Second, a supplier registered as a trading enterprise is generally treated differently from a manufacturer or service provider for these purposes, so confirm the position with your advisor rather than assuming every Udyam number triggers the rule.

children.text: The Clock, and When It Starts

The law sets two limits. Where there is a written agreement, payment is due on the agreed date, and that date cannot exceed 45 days from the day of acceptance. Where there is no written agreement, the limit is 15 days. An agreement for 90-day terms does not override this: the excess simply has no legal effect.

events.title: Goods delivered or services rendered
events.description: This is the day of acceptance, unless the buyer raises a written objection.

events.title: The window to object in writing
events.description: If the buyer objects to the goods or services within 15 days, the day of acceptance moves to the day the objection is resolved, not the day of delivery.

events.title: Payment falls due
events.description: Whatever the purchase order says, the enforceable outer limit is 45 days from acceptance. With no written agreement at all, it is 15 days.

events.title: Statutory interest begins
events.description: Interest runs from the appointed day automatically, at three times the RBI bank rate, compounded monthly. The supplier does not have to demand it for the liability to exist.

events.title: The tax consequence crystallises
events.description: Any amount still unpaid beyond the time limit is disallowed as a deduction for that year, and is allowed only in the year it is actually paid.

body.caption: P is the unpaid principal and n is the number of months of delay. Interest compounds monthly under section 16 of the MSMED Act

children.text: Assume, purely for illustration, that the RBI bank rate is 6%. The statutory rate is then 18% a year, compounded monthly. Check the current bank rate before computing anything for real, because the multiple applies to whatever the rate is at the time.

Take ₹40 lakh owed to a registered micro supplier, paid 90 days beyond the 45-day limit. The statutory interest is about ₹1.83 lakh. The same delay funded at an ordinary commercial rate of 10% would have cost about ₹0.99 lakh, so the statutory liability is roughly 1.85 times as expensive.

body.title: Statutory interest on ₹40 lakh at 18% compounded monthly (₹)
body.xAxisLabel: Months of delay beyond the limit

body.label: The interest you cannot deduct
body.context: Interest paid or payable under the MSMED Act is expressly not allowed as a deduction in computing taxable income. So the true cost is the interest plus the tax you pay on it, not the interest alone.

body.title: Compute the statutory interest
body.prompt: A buyer owes ₹25 lakh to a registered small supplier and pays 60 days beyond the 45-day limit, that is two months late. Assuming an RBI bank rate of 6%, so a statutory rate of 18% a year compounded monthly, what is the interest liability in rupees?
body.explanation: The monthly rate is 18% divided by 12, or 1.5%. Compounded over two months the factor is 1.015 squared, which is 1.030225, so the interest is ₹25,00,000 times 0.030225, about ₹75,562. Note that this liability exists whether or not the supplier raises an invoice for it.

children.text: The Tax Consequence Is the Bigger One

The interest is unpleasant. The tax treatment is what changes behaviour in finance teams. Since the Finance Act, 2023 inserted clause (h) into section 43B of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any amount payable to a micro or small enterprise beyond the MSMED time limit is deductible only in the year of actual payment. The Income-tax Act, 2025 carries the same disallowance forward.

Work through the arithmetic. A company ends the year owing ₹2 crore to micro and small suppliers beyond the time limit. That ₹2 crore is added back to taxable income for the year, costing roughly ₹0.5 crore of tax at an assumed effective rate of about 25%. The deduction returns in the year the supplier is actually paid, so this is a timing difference rather than a permanent loss, but the cash goes out now.

body.text: This is why so many Indian companies run a March payment sweep for micro and small vendors. Paying before the year end converts a disallowance into a deduction, and the cash was owed anyway. If your business has not identified which vendors are covered, that sweep is impossible, which is why the Udyam status belongs in the vendor master and not in somebody's inbox.

body.title: Three more obligations that come with this

children.text: Disclosure in the accounts. A buyer must disclose, in its annual financial statements, the principal and interest due to micro and small enterprises, amounts paid beyond the appointed day, and interest accrued and unpaid. Schedule III separately requires the trade payables ageing schedule to split dues to micro and small enterprises from all others, which you met in Chapter 1.

Reporting in the tax audit. The auditor reports unpaid amounts to micro and small enterprises in Form 3CD, and the disallowance flows from there into the return. This is not a judgement call made by the company alone.

Interest accrues automatically. Section 16 does not require the supplier to claim interest for the liability to arise, and a supplier that waives it in writing today can still pursue it later, since the statutory right is not easily contracted away. Treat any large overdue balance to a micro or small supplier as carrying an unrecorded liability, not as free credit.

body.title: The same rule from both sides of the table

columns.label: If you are the buyer
points: Collect Udyam registration numbers and categories at vendor onboarding, and refresh them annually
Flag micro and small vendors in the payment system so their invoices are scheduled first
Treat 45 days as a hard limit in the purchase order, not an opening position
Run a pre-year-end sweep of overdue micro and small balances
Remember that the interest is not tax deductible, which raises its real cost further

columns.label: If you are the supplier
points: Register on Udyam, since the protection applies only to registered enterprises
Put the Udyam number and the statutory interest clause on every invoice
Track the appointed day for each invoice, because interest runs from it automatically
Use the facilitation council route for delayed payments, which is faster and cheaper than court
Understand that your buyer has a tax reason to pay you before 31 March, and time your follow-up accordingly

body.title: The outer limit
body.textWithBlank: Where a written agreement exists, payment to a registered micro or small enterprise cannot be agreed beyond ___ days from the day of acceptance, and where there is no written agreement the limit is 15 days.
body.explanation: Forty five days is the outer limit under section 15 of the MSMED Act. An agreement for longer terms does not extend it, and interest runs from the day after the limit expires.

body.title: Which of these is outside the payment rule?
body.question: Your company owes money to four suppliers on 31 March. Which one is NOT covered by the MSMED payment timeline?
options: A registered micro enterprise supplying packaging material, 60 days overdue
A registered small enterprise providing machine maintenance, 50 days overdue
A registered medium enterprise supplying castings, 120 days overdue
A registered micro enterprise supplying labels, 46 days overdue
body.explanation: The payment timeline and the tax disallowance apply to micro and small enterprises only. A medium enterprise is outside both, however long the delay runs, which is why the category on the Udyam certificate matters as much as the registration itself.

body.title: A March that arrives badly
body.scenario: It is 12 March. Your payables ledger shows ₹3.8 crore owed to vendors flagged as micro or small, of which ₹2.4 crore is already beyond the 45-day limit. Your cash credit limit has ₹1.1 crore of headroom. The finance head proposes paying whatever the headroom allows and dealing with the rest in April, arguing that the suppliers have not complained and none of them has ever charged interest.
body.prompt: What would you do with the ₹1.1 crore, and what would you tell the finance head?
body.modelAnswer:
Use the headroom deliberately rather than chronologically.

First, rank the ₹2.4 crore of overdue micro and small dues by two things: the size of the balance and how far past the appointed day each one is. Interest compounds monthly, so the oldest large balances are accruing the most, and each one is also carrying a disallowance into the tax computation. Pay the largest overdue balances first until the ₹1.1 crore is exhausted. That converts roughly ₹1.1 crore of disallowance into a deduction and stops the most expensive interest clock.

Second, correct the finance head on two points. Statutory interest accrues whether or not the supplier complains, because the right is statutory rather than contractual, and it is not deductible for tax. And the ₹1.3 crore still unpaid on 31 March will be added back to taxable income, costing roughly ₹33 lakh of tax at about 25%, payable now and recoverable only when the vendors are actually paid.

Third, look for cash that does not need the bank. Chase the receivables over 90 days from Chapter 4 with a specific March target, since collecting ₹1 crore there funds the payment without touching the limit. Ask a few large non-MSME suppliers for a two-week extension, which costs a conversation rather than interest.

Then fix the structural problem in April. This situation exists because micro and small vendors were paid in the same queue as everyone else all year. Flag them in the vendor master, schedule their invoices automatically inside 45 days, and report the overdue micro and small balance monthly rather than discovering it in March.

body.title: Make your business compliant without drama
steps: Collect the Udyam registration number and category from every vendor at onboarding, and refresh it annually.
Record the micro or small flag in the vendor master so it drives the payment schedule automatically.
Set purchase order terms for these vendors at 45 days or less, and stop treating the limit as negotiable.
Date the clock from acceptance, and raise any quality objection in writing within 15 days, since a late objection does not move the appointed day.
Report the overdue micro and small balance to management monthly, not annually.
Run a payment sweep in the first half of March for anything beyond the limit.
Track interest accrued on delayed payments, disclose it in the accounts, and remember it is not tax deductible.
Brief the procurement team, since the negotiation habit of asking for 90-day terms is where most breaches begin.

body.label: Verify a supplier on the Udyam portal
body.description: Ask every vendor for its Udyam certificate, which shows both the registration number and whether the enterprise is micro, small or medium. That single document decides whether the payment rule applies to you.

body.text: For registered micro and small suppliers, payment terms are not a negotiation. Forty five days is the outer limit, interest runs automatically at three times the bank rate compounded monthly, and the deduction disappears until you actually pay.

points: The MSMED Act payment timeline applies to registered micro and small enterprises, not to medium enterprises.
Classification thresholds were revised from 1 April 2025, with micro up to ₹2.5 crore investment and ₹10 crore turnover, and small up to ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore.
The maximum agreed credit period is 45 days from acceptance, or 15 days where there is no written agreement, and a longer agreement does not override this.
Interest runs automatically from the appointed day at three times the RBI bank rate, compounded monthly, whether or not the supplier claims it.
That interest is not deductible for income tax, so its real cost is higher than the rate suggests.
Amounts still unpaid beyond the limit at the year end are disallowed and deductible only when actually paid, which is why March payment sweeps exist.
The whole regime is unusable unless Udyam status sits in the vendor master, so vendor onboarding is where compliance actually happens.
